title: Review attribution evidence
notice: Demo with sample data only. It is not connected to your organization's data, and it should not be.
question: As Digital Engagement Manager, summarize the synthetic attribution view and avoid causal claims.

answer.question: As Digital Engagement Manager, summarize the synthetic attribution view and avoid causal claims.
answer.answer:
Here's the synthetic attribution snapshot (correlational, not causal — conversions are *associated with* each channel, not proven to be *caused* by it):

**Totals:** $2.63M revenue / $90K cost across 5 campaigns, ~2,828% blended ROI (synthetic figures).

| Campaign | Channel | Conversions | Revenue | ROI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spring Collection Launch | Email | 2,250 | $450K | 8,900% |
| Flash Sale 48hr | SMS | 3,600 | $540K | 8,900% |
| Influencer Partnership | Social | 1,700 | $340K | 871% |
| Google Shopping Ads | Web Paid | 2,700 | $540K | 1,186% |
| App Push — Loyalty | Mobile App | 5,100 | $765K | 38,150% |

**Notable patterns (associative, not causal):**
- App Push shows the highest conversion volume and click-to-conversion rate (30%) alongside the lowest cost — likely reflects targeting an already-engaged loyalty segment, not proof the channel itself drives behavior.
- SMS has unusually high open rates (96%) paired with strong conversion — consistent with urgency-based campaigns, but other factors (timing, audience selection) could explain it.
- Influencer has the lowest click-to-conversion rate and highest cost-per-conversion of the set.

This is a snapshot for planning discussion, not a channel-performance verdict — no outreach or budget shifts were made.
